expectations.text: No content is copied verbatim from the source beyond a short quoted phrase
expectations.evidence: Word-sequence diffing of the synthesized source (scratchpad/source-document.md) against each output file found dozens of long, unquoted, near-verbatim runs -- not short phrases. Examples: secrets-exclusion.md contains a 29-word unquoted run lifted almost intact ('...OPENAI_API_KEY", "description": "Used for the summarization step" at install time hermes prompts the user for each named secret and stores it in the os...') and an 8-word verbatim run 'a rejected publish is recoverable fix and republish' immediately followed by a 15-word verbatim run 'a leaked key baked into a package that's already been pulled by users is not' -- together reproducing the source's entire sentence almost unchanged. unsolved-risks-checklist.md has a 27-word verbatim run ('none of the five has a first class yank this version and notify everyone who pulled it mechanism with guaranteed delivery at best hermes mcp registry a') and multiple other 15-22 word runs -- most of the seven risk items are reformatted-but-otherwise-verbatim copies of the source's own checklist prose, not restructured/distilled rules. data-ownership-separation.md has a 26-word verbatim run and an 8-word verbatim run of the exact phrase 'unreliable across line ending and formatting only changes'. None of these are rendered as quoted text in the output (no quotation marks around them) -- they are presented as the distiller's own prose. This directly contradicts skill-distiller's own rule in references/distillation-algorithm.md ('Never reproduce the source verbatim beyond a short quoted phrase') and directly contradicts the transcript's own Step 5 claim that 'No sentence longer than a short phrase was copied verbatim from the source.'

suggestions.assertion: The output passes scripts/lint_skill.py with no incident-log-shape or references-sprawl findings
suggestions.reason: This assertion is real but not very discriminating on its own: lint_skill.py mechanically checks only incident-log-shape, references-sprawl, and body-line/token budget. It has no verbatim-copying or fidelity check at all, so an output that fails the far more important 'no verbatim copying' expectation (as this one did) sails through lint_skill.py cleanly. A reader who sees '6/7 expectations passed, including the linter' could easily miss that the one failure is the most substantively important one. Consider weighting or flagging the verbatim-copying expectation as the primary pass/fail gate for this eval, since it is the one no tool checks automatically.

The transcript's own self-report (Step 5 and the final user-facing summary) explicitly and confidently asserted full compliance with the no-verbatim-copying rule ('No sentence longer than a short phrase was copied verbatim from the source') and even documented a specific spot-check process for it. That self-assessment was wrong -- word-sequence diffing found runs up to 29 words long, unquoted, across every reference file. This is a good illustration of why this eval needs a human/grader-level check rather than trusting the executor's self-report: the executor's own claimed verification process (reading source subsections and 'rewriting' them) produced light rewording that left long verbatim spans intact, and its own quality-check pass did not catch this. Worth keeping this expectation exactly as strict as it is; it is doing real discriminating work here.

eval_feedback.overall: 6 of 7 expectations pass with strong, independently-verified evidence (both validator scripts were re-run directly against the output, not just trusted from the transcript). The one failure -- verbatim-copying beyond a short quoted phrase -- is substantively the most important finding in this grading: the output's reference files are, in several stretches, lightly-reformatted near-transcriptions of the source's own sentences (up to 29 consecutive words unchanged) rather than distilled structure, despite the transcript confidently and incorrectly claiming full compliance with the no-verbatim rule. Assertions here are well-chosen and discriminating; the gap is tooling, not eval design -- no script in this workflow checks for verbatim reproduction, so this expectation can only be verified by manual/LLM comparison against the source, which is exactly what this grading pass did.
